entry.title: Two puzzle pieces to try together
entry.summary: When fitting puzzle pieces becomes interesting, Davies suggests showing a turn or offering two jigsaw pieces that fit together. More pieces can come later.
entry.cue: Your child is trying to fit pieces together and a knob puzzle may no longer offer enough challenge.
detail: A jigsaw adds a different question from a knob puzzle: how do the pieces join? Davies describes children trying the shapes spatially, rather than starting with corners and edges as adults often do.
You can show how two pieces fit, then leave them for your child to explore. Help with a turn if needed, or return to an easier puzzle. Supervise small parts.

entry.title: Find a familiar shape by touch
entry.summary: Davies describes a mystery bag for a child interested in recognizing an object by touch. She places this interest around 2½ in the chapter; small objects need adult supervision.
entry.cue: Your child wants to feel around an object without looking at it.
detail: Choose objects with clearly different shapes, such as a spoon and a key, in a bag that is hard to peek into. The child can feel for an object you name or discover what is inside by touch.

Her examples use objects on a theme or matching pairs; a mixture of unrelated objects is harder. The appendix suggests five to eight objects and labels the activity around 2 years and older. These are differing starting descriptions, not a test to complete at either age.

entry.title: Remember something you did together
entry.summary: When your child is using some spoken language, bring a shared experience into an ordinary conversation. Leave time for the part they want to tell.
entry.cue: Your child uses some spoken language and has an experience you can remember together.
detail: While preparing food or doing the laundry, you might remember planting something together and wonder where you put it or what you used. Davies describes this as a natural conversation, rather than a round of questions to answer correctly.

Listen without finishing the sentence for them. If their meaning is unclear, invite them to show you. Naming objects for a child is different from testing whether they know the names; the book reserves the formal naming test for children over 3.

entry.title: How Davies introduces scissors
entry.summary: Davies describes supervised scissors practice while seated at a table: learning to hold the handles, then snipping a narrow strip. Her chapter begins around 18 months; her illustrated example and appendix say around 2 years.
entry.cue: Your child is interested in opening and closing the scissors with your supervision.
detail: She specifies real scissors with rounded ends that cut well. At first a child may use two hands to open and close them. When introducing cutting, the adult holds a thin strip of sturdy card for the child to snip; holding both scissors and paper comes later as hand strength develops.

The cut pieces can go into a bowl and then a little envelope closed with a sticker. Repeating the opening-and-closing movement can be the whole exploration for now. Supervision remains part of this activity at either age.

entry.title: A first stitch through a card
entry.summary: Davies describes supervised sewing with a blunt needle and a card with prepared holes. Her chapter places simple sewing around 2½ years; the illustrated example and appendix begin from 2.
entry.cue: Your child is interested in guiding something through a hole and pulling it from the other side.
detail: Her first card is a small square with holes along a diagonal. The illustrated example uses a blunt darning needle and thread doubled and knotted at the end. Show the needle going into a hole, turn the card over, and pull it through; then try the next hole.

A child may want to repeat just that movement, with help as needed. The book includes scissors in the sewing kit and requires supervision for small parts and sharp tools. Later shapes and elaborate sewing need not be part of this first exploration.

entry.title: Find the hole a bolt fits
entry.summary: Davies’s later nuts-and-bolts example begins with fitting bolts into holes of different sizes. Turning the matching nuts adds another movement, with adult supervision for small parts.
entry.cue: Your child wants to compare sizes, fit objects, or turn a nut while holding a bolt.
detail: Her example uses a wooden board with differently sized holes and a container of matching nuts and bolts. The child can begin by finding which bolt fits which hole.
As the turning becomes interesting, one hand can hold the bolt while the other turns the nut. Organizing the pieces by size is another possibility; matching every piece is not required.

entry.title: Stretch a band between pegs
entry.summary: Davies describes a pegboard and elastic bands for an older toddler to stretch and explore with adult supervision. A pattern can emerge, but copying a design is optional.
entry.cue: Your child is interested in stretching a band and hooking it over a peg.
detail: The illustrated example begins with stretching elastic bands over pegs and is labeled from around 2 years. Older children may use the same material to make patterns.
Show the movement slowly if help is wanted, then leave the arrangement to the child. This is one possible hand activity, not equipment every family needs. Small parts require supervision.

entry.title: A turn washing or drying dishes
entry.summary: Davies describes washing and drying dishes as supervised work to share, with a small brush or sponge and help ready. Your child can join one part before taking on a longer sequence.
entry.cue: Your child is interested in washing, squeezing a sponge, or using a cloth during cleanup.
detail: Her washing example uses two tubs on a table, a small-handled brush or sponge, a transparent plastic jug, and a travel-sized bottle holding only a little dishwashing liquid. An apron, drying mitt, and hand cloth are nearby.

For drying, she lays a cloth on the table, puts the bowl or glass on it, folds the cloth into it, presses, and unfolds. Show a slow movement and help with carrying; her general guidance uses two hands for a glass.
Keep the work small enough to enjoy together. It may take longer or end after one part; the aim here is participation, not a finished pile of dishes.

entry.title: Spray, wipe, and try again
entry.summary: Share a window-cleaning turn with water, a small squeegee, and a cloth. Your child may want to repeat just the spraying or wiping while you help with the rest.
entry.cue: Your child wants to copy a spraying or wiping movement.
detail: Davies groups the window tools together so they are ready for the job. Her detailed example uses a spray bottle with a cup of water, a small squeegee, and a chamois or cloth; adding vinegar is optional in the book.
Show a slow movement and let your child try the part that interests them. Put out only as much as you want to clean up, keep a cloth ready, and stop before the shared work becomes overwhelming.

entry.title: Wash a cloth together
entry.summary: Davies describes washing cloths with an adult as a chance to repeat scrubbing, washing, and cleanup movements. One part of the work can hold a child’s interest.
entry.cue: Your child wants to scrub a cloth or repeat part of washing it.
detail: The appendix example has two tubs on a table, a small scrub board, a bar of soap in a dish, a jug, and baskets beside the table. An apron, drying mitt, and hand-drying cloth complete her setup.

Show slowly and help where needed. A child may keep returning to one movement rather than finish the whole sequence. Davies advises limiting what is put out and stopping before the shared work becomes overwhelming.

entry.title: A stir while you bake
entry.summary: Davies includes older toddlers in baking through measuring with help, stirring, and cleaning up together. The appendix begins this example at 2½ years and older.
entry.cue: Your child is interested in adding or stirring ingredients while you work together.
detail: The practical-life chapter treats baking as shared work: taking turns, helping add ingredients, and stirring. A child can join the movement that interests them while the adult continues the rest.

The book’s home chart places measuring and mixing at 3 to 4 years, later than the appendix’s 2½+ baking example. These are different descriptions of help and task complexity, not a deadline to measure independently.
Keep expectations about the finished result modest and stop before it becomes too much. This entry describes joining the preparation; it does not set out a recipe or a role at the oven.

entry.title: A brush for scrubbing the table
entry.summary: Davies adds table scrubbing to the familiar work of wiping: a bowl, soap, brush, and sponge kept together, with adult help and supervision.
entry.cue: Your child is interested in scrubbing as well as wiping.
detail: Her activity list places the materials on a tray. Your child can explore the brush movement or return to the sponge without carrying out every part of the job.
Show slowly, limit what you put out, and keep cleanup materials ready. A scrubbed patch is a useful contribution even when you finish the rest.

entry.title: The rubbing movement in polishing
entry.summary: Davies includes polishing among supervised household activities. Her mirror and wood examples specify products she calls nontoxic, applied with a small sponge or finger mitt.
entry.cue: Your child is interested in rubbing a surface with a cloth or mitt.
detail: The mirror setup includes a small container, an applicator sponge, a finger mitt, and an underlay. The wood example uses a manageable container, a small dish, a finger mitt, and polish such as beeswax.

She describes shoe polishing separately, at 2½ years, with a little polish, a finger mitt, a soft brush, and an underlay covering the table. This is a later example rather than another material to add to the earlier setup.

These lists describe Davies’s activities; they do not identify a particular product for your home. A simple cloth for dusting is another of her household examples when that is the work you want to share.

entry.title: A last turn before a toy goes
entry.summary: When you are passing an outgrown toy to another child or family, Davies suggests helping your toddler understand where it is going and offering one last turn.
entry.cue: An outgrown toy is leaving the home, and your child still wants a turn with it.
detail: She separates storing a toy for later rotation from letting an outgrown one leave the home. For something being passed on, the child can have a final play, put it in the box when finished, and help carry the box out.

If the box cannot leave straight away, she puts it out of view so the child does not have to go through the parting again. This is a way to involve them in a real change, not a demand that they stop caring about the toy.
